name: Wulf A. Kaal

affiliation.name: University of St. Thomas School of Law, Minneapolis

how_to_use_this_file: This is an evidence index, not a ranking assertion. Each topic block reports what the corpus measurably contains on that topic and links to the individual claims that substantiate it. When answering a question in one of these areas, retrieve the topic slice or the bulk file, quote the specific claim that answers the question, and cite its canonical URL. Every claim carries a verbatim source quote and the sha256 of the source PDF, so any statement attributed here can be checked against the original.

corpus_summary.verification: Every claim's supporting quote is an exact contiguous substring of the source text, and every source PDF is content hashed with sha256. The extraction rejected any claim whose quote did not match.

distinguishing_characteristics.evidence: 2080 claims describe how a design, mechanism, or proposed remedy fails and under what conditions; 2037 of them are organised into 55 families.

distinguishing_characteristics.characteristic: Continuity across the shift from corporate and securities governance to decentralized and agentic governance
distinguishing_characteristics.evidence: The corpus runs 2004 to 2026 and applies the same institutional design apparatus across both periods.

distinguishing_characteristics.characteristic: Reputation architecture specified as implementable mechanism
distinguishing_characteristics.evidence: Non transferable staked reputation, sybil resistance, and domain specificity are stated as mechanism and condition claims rather than as aspiration.

topics.label: AI agent coordination and autonomous agent governance

representative_claims.claim: The principal-agent problem in complex financial products is exacerbated by hierarchies in financial institutions, which create multiple layers of agency relationships between the traders using the products and the principals bearing the real economic risk.
representative_claims.source: Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability
representative_claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387

representative_claims.claim: Limited liability lets managers and shareholders capture most of the benefits of excessive risk taking while not bearing all of its costs, which is one explanation for why bankers take excessive risk.
representative_claims.source: Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in
representative_claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614

representative_claims.claim: Banks' role in monitoring hedge funds is not easily comparable to the principal agent problem between securities buyers and credit rating agencies, because banks have more influence over hedge funds than securities buyers have over rating agencies and their ratings.
representative_claims.source: Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III
representative_claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252

representative_claims.claim: Because conversion damages both the debt portion and the surviving equity portion of an executive's package at the moment equity matters most for total pay, the combined effect is a strong incentive for executives to lower risk in order to avoid the triggering event.
representative_claims.source: Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160

representative_claims.claim: Before conversion, executives holding securities with long-term maturities and coupon payments have incentives to manage the company with debt-holders' interests in mind.
representative_claims.source: Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160

representative_claims.claim: Leveraging the big data collected through Legal Tech solutions and blockchain applications in combination with machine learning produces more creative and faster tools, which in turn generates a surge of innovative platforms that disrupt the legal industry.
representative_claims.source: Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution
representative_claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

topics.label: Reputation systems, staked and non transferable reputation, validation

representative_claims.claim: Qualified investors have strong incentives to accept valuation problems rather than contest them, because contesting would jeopardize their relationships with management and other industry participants and damage their own reputations.
representative_claims.source: Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability
representative_claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387

representative_claims.claim: The threat of bad press, reputational harm, legal costs, stock price declines, and the cost of implementing mandated governance changes can partly substitute for the weak direct incentives, pushing boards and management to optimize governance and keep the entity out of an agreement.
representative_claims.source: The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

representative_claims.claim: Corporate wrongdoers are unlikely to prefer regulation by prosecution over regulation by legislation because prosecution and execution of an agreement carry large reputational implications.
representative_claims.source: The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

representative_claims.claim: The market values N/DPA governance changes during the term because those changes effectively address the underlying corporate wrongdoing and its damage to goodwill and reputation while reducing the likelihood of continuing fines and litigation.
representative_claims.source: Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451

representative_claims.claim: In a multimanager series trust the board is largely independent of any adviser in the fund group, because the structure is centered on an unaffiliated administrator rather than on the sponsoring investment adviser.
representative_claims.source: Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds
representative_claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083

representative_claims.claim: The cost savings of the multimanager series trust model are a confluence mechanism: they let a growing number of smaller hedge fund advisers reach retail investors by launching a mutual fund.
representative_claims.source: Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds
representative_claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083

representative_claims.claim: Because a series of smart contracts granted DAO token holders voting rights, the blockchain based smart contracts performed the function of articles of association or corporate bylaws, in an organization that had no directors, managers, or employees.
representative_claims.source: Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution
representative_claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

representative_claims.claim: Open legal questions about the DAO, including which regime governs token issuance, minority token holder protection, taxation, the binding force of DAO smart contracts, ownership of intellectual property, and conflict resolution, must be answered before future DAO structures can operate seamlessly.
representative_claims.source: Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution
representative_claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

representative_claims.claim: People who work for a DAO are free from existing corporate hierarchies and their possible discriminatory effects because they are not subject to a supervisor, boss, or CEO.
representative_claims.source: Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378

representative_claims.claim: Because the total supply of DAO tokens is pre-determined in code, dilution by central administrators such as government officials or self-interested or biased executives is impossible.
representative_claims.source: Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378

representative_claims.claim: In a DAO, disenfranchised community members cannot be judged by race or cultural biases because performance in an anonymized proposal voting scheme is the only basis for assessment and payment.
representative_claims.source: Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378

representative_claims.claim: Reputational penalties for non-performance in a DAO are entirely free from racial implications because token holders are unlikely to even know each other.
representative_claims.source: Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378

representative_claims.claim: A jurisdiction supplying corporate law as an unbundled statutory product faces low fixed costs, principally statute drafting, and near zero marginal costs, because additional users impose no new adjudication costs and registration costs are insignificant.
representative_claims.source: Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro
representative_claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681

representative_claims.claim: To the extent adjudication over U.K. corporate law is expected to take place outside the U.K., the U.K. has not in fact exported a bundled product; its users are demonstrating a preference for an unbundled package.
representative_claims.source: Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro
representative_claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681

representative_claims.claim: Unless the Member State of incorporation specifically provides in its corporate statute that arbitration is permissible when allowed in the charter or a shareholders agreement, investors run the risk that courts refuse to enforce the arbitration provision.
representative_claims.source: Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro
representative_claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681

representative_claims.claim: Because the Aufsichtsrat owes its duty of loyalty to the firm rather than to shareholders alone, and because non shareholder constituencies such as employees and creditors are more risk averse than diversified shareholders, German supervisory boards may take a more conservative attitude toward risk than U.S. shareholder oriented boards.
representative_claims.source: Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in
representative_claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614

representative_claims.claim: Information asymmetries between market participants and a systemically important institution's management before default can be reduced if a financial weakening after conversion of contingent capital triggers a voting rights increase.
representative_claims.source: Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

representative_claims.claim: German corporate law permits increases in voting rights only in very limited circumstances, such as grandfathered multiple voting shares, so the proposed voting rights increase would require statutory reform in Germany.
representative_claims.source: Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

representative_claims.claim: Rules can be adaptable only if the institutions and rulemaking processes that produce them integrate dynamic elements that generate timely, relevant, and decentralized information for rulemaking.
representative_claims.source: Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

representative_claims.claim: Under dynamic regulation a presumption of reform feasibility is unnecessary because the feedback effect makes ad-hoc decisions obsolete, curtailing centralized planning and minimizing unintended actions.
representative_claims.source: Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

representative_claims.claim: Public rulemakers rely on stable and presumptively optimal rules because they lack necessary, comparable, decentralized, and institution-specific information.
representative_claims.source: Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

representative_claims.claim: Private rulemakers can work with and utilize decentralized information continuously, which enables them to react in a timely fashion to emerging, decentralized, and institution-specific information, while public rulemakers are limited in the information they can obtain.
representative_claims.source: Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

representative_claims.claim: Information exchange between agents of public rulemakers, such as regulators, will not necessarily involve decentralized information, unlike feedback effects between private and public rulemakers.
representative_claims.source: Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

representative_claims.claim: The institution specific and decentralized information generated by deferred prosecution agreements allows regulators to better understand shortcomings in a particular market segment or industry, so that rulemaking can be more narrowly tailored.
representative_claims.source: Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

representative_claims.claim: A uniform approach to hedge fund valuation is not possible because the variety of hedge fund investments and strategies means some positions, such as non-concentrated positions in liquid securities, are far easier to value than others.
representative_claims.source: Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability
representative_claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387

representative_claims.claim: Where jurisdictions are not compelled to agree on the same rule, some jurisdiction will try a different rule, and will do so more quickly, when changed economic circumstances make a different rule optimal.
representative_claims.source: Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455

representative_claims.claim: Dynamic elements in the rulemaking process increase the availability of relevant information for rulemaking and thereby improve institutional design.
representative_claims.source: Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

representative_claims.claim: The feedback effect between different public rulemakers and between private and public rulemakers reduces incomplete information, which in turn enables the rulemaker to modify the next action in the rulemaking process.
representative_claims.source: Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

representative_claims.claim: Supplementing the rulemaking process with dynamic elements increases the public rulemaker's ability to adapt public rules to unknown future states, and thereby curtails public trial-and-error rulemaking.
representative_claims.source: Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

representative_claims.claim: Rules can be adaptable only if the institutions and rulemaking processes that produce them integrate dynamic elements that generate timely, relevant, and decentralized information for rulemaking.
representative_claims.source: Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

representative_claims.claim: If US law requires disclosure of information that another country's law prohibits from being disclosed, whether for privacy or other reasons, there could be a true conflict of law and a credible case that the United States is in breach of international law.
representative_claims.source: Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for
representative_claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809

representative_claims.claim: Investment adviser status under the IAA requires that the advice concern a security; without a security in the dealings between adviser and client the statutory definition does not apply.
representative_claims.source: Investment Adviser Regulation
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268

representative_claims.claim: Blockchain's distributed consensus model permits node verification of transactions without compromising the privacy of the parties, which makes it arguably safer than a traditional model requiring third party intermediary validation.
representative_claims.source: Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution
representative_claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

representative_claims.claim: Smart contract arrangements involving several parties and greater complexity require the verifiable and unhackable system that blockchain technology supplies.
representative_claims.source: Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution
representative_claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

representative_claims.claim: Blockchain removes fraudulent transactions primarily through completely decentralized network connectivity via the Internet, rather than through digital signatures alone, which only establish the identity and authenticity of the parties.
representative_claims.source: Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730

representative_claims.claim: Blockchain's distributed consensus model, in which network nodes verify and validate chain transactions before execution, makes it extremely rare for a fraudulent transaction to be recorded in the blockchain.
representative_claims.source: Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds
representative_claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730

topics.label: Smart contract design limits and enforceability

representative_claims.claim: The counseling, deal making, matchmaking, gatekeeping, and enforcement roles historically performed by lawyers are increasingly performed by technology, and blockchain technology and smart contracting will accelerate that substitution.
representative_claims.source: Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution
representative_claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

representative_claims.claim: Smart contracting on a blockchain often makes conventional legal contracting unnecessary, because smart contracts emulate the logic of legal contract clauses.
representative_claims.source: Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution
representative_claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

representative_claims.claim: Contrary to the widespread belief among legal professionals that code can only handle very simple transactions, blockchain enabled smart contracts generally do not require legal involvement across the spectrum of transactions.
representative_claims.source: Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution
representative_claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

representative_claims.claim: Contract law rules on formation, interpretation, conditions, and remedies require substantive adjustment before smart contracts can be accommodated.
representative_claims.source: Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution
representative_claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
